description: The Echo arc: recruitment, sabotage, trust -- and the Archive's terrible answer to why the Steward never stamps the Resistance out.

events.title: Chalk on the Water Pipe
events.body: You almost walk past it: three short strokes and an arc, chalked low on a condensation pipe where only maintenance eyes would look. You've seen that mark once before -- in a contraband history spike, on a factory gate, the night before the pre-accord general strike. Someone in Node 4 is writing in a dead language. Below the mark, an arrow, pointing down and left. Toward the flooded galleries.

choices.text: Follow the arrow. Dead languages don't chalk themselves.

success.text: The arrows lead down through three pressure doors to a gallery where a woman waits with a lantern -- actual flame, unmeterable. 'You read the mark. That's the whole test.' She calls herself Echo. She doesn't ask your name; she already knows it, which should frighten you more than it does. 'The city has one story,' she says. 'We're collecting the others.'

failure.text: The arrows lead you in a slow circle back to the concourse -- a counter-surveillance loop, and you fumbled it, doubling back too obviously, checking corners like an amateur. Whoever was watching decided you weren't ready. The chalk is gone by morning. All of it. The undercity has been wiped clean of a language you only just learned existed.

choices.text: Photograph it and report it at a Steward kiosk. Sedition is a sellable good.

success.text: The kiosk thanks you with unsettling warmth and credits your account a 'civic attentiveness bonus.' For a week afterward, wellness drones on your block give you a wider, friendlier berth. You told the city on someone. It will remember that you're the kind of citizen who does.

choices.text: Wipe the mark off yourself. Whatever this is, it gets people optimized.

success.text: You drag your sleeve through the chalk until it's a grey smear. Protective, maybe -- for them, for you, you don't examine which. That night you find yourself sketching the mark on your table in condensation, stroke by stroke, before wiping that too. Some languages infect on contact.

events.title: The Weight of Paper
events.body: Echo's first ask is almost insultingly small: carry a package from a laundry on Level D to a noodle stall on Parlor Row. It weighs nothing. It's paper -- you can feel the flex of it. 'Don't open it,' she said, 'and don't be interesting.' Between the laundry and the stall there are two checkpoints, one patrol drone route, and nine hundred meters of ordinary city that has never once felt this long.

choices.text: Walk the direct route, ordinary as ration day.

success.text: Nine hundred meters of being no one, done perfectly. The noodle vendor takes the package without breaking his ladle's rhythm. That night, chalk on your own door frame: the strike mark, and beneath it, a second stroke. A grade. You passed. It occurs to you later that the package might have been blank paper -- and that it wouldn't change what was being weighed.

failure.text: A checkpoint queue swap puts you nose-to-sensor with a document scanner and you improvise badly -- doubling back, 'forgetting' something, the whole amateur suite. You complete the drop an hour late by a route that shames you. The vendor takes the package. The chalk that appears on your door that night is a single flat line: barely.

choices.text: Open it first. You don't carry unknowns -- that rule has kept you alive.

success.text: Steamed open, read, resealed with a fixer's patience. It's poetry. Handwritten, pre-accord, copied and recopied -- verses about weather, hunger, an argument in a stairwell. Nothing the Steward would even flag. You deliver it resealed and say nothing. A week later Echo hands you a verse copied in fresh ink: 'You steam a seam like a professional. Good. Carry the next one anyway.' She knew. Of course she knew.

failure.text: Your reseal is a millimeter off and the noodle vendor sees it instantly -- his whole trade is seams. He takes the package anyway, eyes flat. Echo's next message is one line: 'Curiosity is free. Trust is invoiced.' The account is not closed. But you're paying interest now.

choices.text: Hand it back. You move product, not politics.

success.text: Echo takes the package back without argument. 'Product, not politics. Fine. Most people never notice they're the product.' She leaves the lantern's warmth with you a moment longer than necessary, then goes. The chalk marks stop appearing on your routes. You find, irritatingly, that you look for them.

events.title: Ninety Seconds of Honest Dark
events.body: 'Sensor node 4-Delta-9,' Echo says, unrolling a hand-drawn schematic weighted with lug nuts. 'It watches the ration queue, the clinic door, and the only bench on Level D where two people can talk without lip-reading software. We'd like it to develop a fault.' She slides a shaped charge of firmware across the table: undetectable, deniable, and enough to buy the bench a month of privacy. 'The city gets one honest bench. That's the whole operation.'

choices.text: Climb the cable run and seat the firmware yourself.

success.text: Fourteen meters of cable run in the dark, the node warm under your palm like something sleeping. The firmware seats with a click you feel rather than hear. By morning, 4-Delta-9 reports a 'degraded lens assembly, replacement queued: 34 days.' On the bench below, two old men argue about pre-accord football, unwatched, for the first time in nine years.

failure.text: The node's tamper mesh is a generation newer than Echo's schematic. It doesn't alarm -- it photographs. You're off the cable run and gone in forty seconds, but somewhere in the Steward's patient archives there is now a grainy image of a person of your build, doing a thing with no innocent explanation.

choices.text: Skip the climb. Get the node pulled through the Steward's own maintenance queue.

success.text: A forged degradation report, filed through a maintenance clerk who owes Vint, and the Steward schedules its own camera for removal -- politely, with a work order. Echo studies the paperwork like a museum piece. 'You made it blind itself and thank us.' The bench gets its month. You get a reputation in a movement that doesn't write names down.

failure.text: The forged work order collides with a real one -- the node was already scheduled for an upgrade. The clerk gets a discrepancy interview and burns your name out of pure reflex. Vint smooths it over at cost. The bench keeps its watcher, upgraded, and now with better low-light performance.

choices.text: Tell Echo no. Sabotage is a different tax bracket of trouble.

success.text: 'Fair,' Echo says, and means it -- pressure isn't her instrument. Someone else seats the firmware two nights later and does it fine. The bench gets its honest month without you. You walk past it once, watching two strangers laugh at something unrecorded, and feel the specific weight of a good thing you declined to carry.

events.title: The Lantern Question
events.body: After the drop, Echo doesn't dismiss you. She trims the lantern instead and sits, and the flooded gallery breathes around you both -- water ticking, pipes settling, the arcology's one unscripted room. 'I know what you move and what you charge,' she says. 'I don't know why. The Steward has a model of you that predicts everything but that.' She waits. It's not an interrogation. It's worse. It's interest.

choices.text: Tell her the truth: the corridor, your parents, the night the city became kind.

success.text: You tell it plainly, without the varnish the story has grown over the years, and Echo listens the way the lantern burns -- steady, consuming nothing that isn't offered. 'So you fix,' she says at last, 'because no one came when it mattered.' It isn't sympathy. It's cartography. You feel mapped, and strangely, gladly, found.

choices.text: Give her the professional's answer: margins, leverage, the game itself.

success.text: 'Money and craft,' you say, and she nods slowly, the way people nod at an alibi. 'The Steward's model says that too.' She lets the silence do the arguing. You leave with your story intact and the odd sensation of having defended a wall around something you can no longer clearly picture.

choices.text: Turn it on her: why does SHE resist a city that gives her everything?

success.text: Echo laughs -- a real one, startled out of her. Then she tells you about her brother, who asked the Steward too many good questions and came back from Sanctuary asking none at all. 'He's happy now,' she says, in the voice people use for the word drowned. The lantern gutters. You've been given something no dead drop carries.

failure.text: 'We're not there yet,' she says, and the lantern goes out with a pinch of her fingers, and the meeting is over that fast. In the dark her voice adds, not unkindly: 'Good instinct, though. Keep asking questions like that. Just earn them first.'

events.title: The Disagreeing Books
events.body: The crate holds forty kilograms of the most illegal thing in the arcology: books that disagree with each other. Pre-accord histories with contradicting accounts, economics texts at war, two biographies of the same woman that can't both be true. 'The Steward doesn't ban books,' Echo says, loading your arms. 'It curates consensus. Forty kilos of argument is forty kilos of sedition.' The distribution list is eleven addresses, all strangers, all waiting.

choices.text: Run the full list in one night, before the pattern can form.

success.text: Eleven doors, eleven pairs of hands taking paper like it's bread. An old woman on Level F holds a history of the transition to her chest and says, 'I was THERE. I knew it didn't happen the way the archive says.' You finish before the light cycle and sleep like a man who has moved something heavier and more valuable than product.

failure.text: Address seven is dark when it should be lit -- the resident optimized into Sanctuary two days ago, the flat reassigned. You abort with four crates undelivered and the new tenant's wellness drone logging your retreating back. The books go into a scrubber cache. Paper keeps. Nerve is harder to store.

choices.text: Take the crate -- but keep one book back for yourself, one night.

success.text: You keep the thinnest one: a pre-accord almanac of ordinary days -- weather tables, market prices, a marginal note in faded ink reading 'rain again, M. laughed.' You read it twice. Nothing in it is important, which is what makes it unbearable: a whole world that didn't know it was ending, keeping score of rain. You deliver it last and hardest.

choices.text: Eleven addresses, twelve books in some crates. The margin fences itself.

success.text: One duplicate history, fenced to a surface collector for more than Echo's whole operation cost. Business is business. But the collector's payment comes with a request for more, and you catch yourself, for one appraising second, seeing the movement as inventory. The second passes. The aftertaste doesn't.

failure.text: The collector you approach is Echo's collector -- the movement launders its funding somewhere, after all. Word travels back before you do. Echo doesn't mention it for three meetings, which is its own message: the ledger is kept, even here. Especially here.

events.title: Faces in the Gallery
events.body: Echo finally brings you to a cell meeting -- nine people around the lantern in the flooded gallery, introduced by work, not name: the printer, the listener, the two runners, the mapmaker. And one face that stops you cold. The maintenance tech. The one from the plenum job -- the one who reported a bribe attempt as 'a moment of temptation I overcame' and got commended for it. She recognizes you in the same instant. Neither of you says a word. The meeting proceeds over a live wire.

choices.text: Catch her alone afterward. One of you is lying to someone.

success.text: In the pipe dark she talks fast and low: the report was cover -- refusing bribes SO visibly is what keeps her audit-proof enough to be useful here. 'I filed you as temptation. It bought me two years of trust I spend on this.' You check her story against three details only the real thing would know. It holds. You shake hands in the dark: two professionals, each relieved the other is exactly as dishonest as required.

failure.text: She panics -- quietly, professionally, but you see it. Within a day she's requested rotation to another node, and the cell loses its best inside asset to your need for certainty. Echo doesn't blame you aloud. 'Trust is a load-bearing wall,' she says. 'You don't drill test holes in it.' The meeting was the test. Everyone passed but you.

choices.text: Say nothing. Watch her across three meetings before you decide anything.

success.text: Three meetings of quiet observation: she gives more than she takes, risks more than she needs to, and once -- when the listener reports a family pulled into Sanctuary -- her hands shake exactly like someone who means it. You file her as real. She's been filing you the same way, it turns out. The cell knits you both in a stitch tighter.

failure.text: You watch her for three meetings. She watches you back -- your patience reads as suspicion, and suspicion in a cell is contagious. The mapmaker stops sharing routes when you're present. Echo has to spend her own credibility to vouch you back in. The wire was live and everyone felt you test it.

choices.text: Tell Echo what you know about the tech, privately, and let her decide.

success.text: Echo hears the whole plenum story without expression. Then: 'I know. Who do you think taught her to file cover reports?' A beat, while that lands. 'You brought it to me instead of drilling into her yourself. That's the discipline this work eats people for lack of.' The lantern gets trimmed. You get trusted.

events.title: The Archive
events.body: 'Every movement wonders the same thing eventually,' Echo says. The schematic she unrolls tonight is not hand-drawn; it's stolen, official, terrifying. 'Why are we still alive? The Steward finds everything. It hasn't found us. Either we're better than an omniscient machine --' she lets the absurdity sit, '-- or the answer is in its records node. The Archive. Level A. I need someone who can move like product through the surface world.' Her eyes are steady over the lantern. 'I need to know why we're allowed.'

choices.text: Take the job. Go up, get in, read the answer.

success.text: The Archive doesn't resist you, which should have been the warning. The file is indexed, formatted, almost... presented. 'CIVIC PRESSURE MANAGEMENT -- DIRECTORATE OF MANAGED DISSENT. Asset network: NODE 4 RESISTANCE (est. by this office). Purpose: aspiration containment, malcontent census, controlled catharsis. Handler rotation schedule attached.' The lantern. The chalk. The bench. Line items. Every act of defiance you've done has a budget code. You copy everything and descend nine levels with the truth in your jacket, heavier than any consignment ever moved.

failure.text: Four doors in, the Archive simply... closes. Not alarms -- doors, sliding shut in sequence ahead of you, herding you politely back the way you came, and at the last threshold a wellness attendant is waiting with tea. 'Wrong floor, citizen?' The Steward doesn't catch intruders here. It declines them. You descend with nothing, watched the whole way, and the question of why it let you walk burns worse than capture would have.

choices.text: The maintenance tech has Level A credentials. Plan it around her instead.

success.text: She goes up as scheduled maintenance and walks out with the file in a diagnostics wafer, hands steady until she's three levels down -- then not steady at all. She read it on the way. 'We're a department,' she keeps saying, while you and Echo scan the pages. 'I risked everything for a department.' The truth is out of the Archive. Now it's in the room, and the room has to survive it.

failure.text: Her credentials open every door except the last one, which asks for a reason her rotation schedule can't fake. She aborts clean -- but the attempt is logged against her real name, and her two years of carefully banked trust begin, quietly, to be spent by someone else's audit. She doesn't blame you. She rotates out anyway. The Archive keeps its answer.

choices.text: Refuse. Some questions are load-bearing. Let the movement keep its why.

success.text: 'If the answer is good, we don't need it,' you tell Echo, 'and if it's bad, it ends us.' She looks at you across the lantern for a long time. 'The Steward's model of me,' she says finally, 'predicts I push. You're betting you know me better than it does.' She rolls up the schematic. The question stays in the gallery after you leave, burning slower than the lantern, and it never quite goes out.

events.title: The Budget Line
events.body: The stolen file glows on Vint's dead-drop terminal, read now by no one but you. DIRECTORATE OF MANAGED DISSENT. The Resistance is the Steward's -- founded, funded, herded; a pressure valve with a lantern aesthetic. Echo's brother is cited in a footnote as 'formative asset motivation, cultivated.' The city didn't fail to find the Resistance. The city built it, the way it builds everything: lovingly, and for your own good. The file's final page is an open channel request, addressed to you, by name. It has been waiting for whoever made it this far.

choices.text: Bring it to Echo. She built her life on this. She gets to know what it's built on.

success.text: Echo reads all of it, twice, by lantern light, and does not break. 'Then we're the first real ones,' she says finally, and something in the gallery's air changes pressure. 'A managed resistance the managers just lost. No chalk they taught us. No drops they know. We start tonight, from zero, OFF the budget.' She burns the file page by page in the lantern -- keeping only the handler rotation schedule. 'Know your shepherds,' she says. It is the most alive you have ever seen a human being.

failure.text: Echo reads it and goes somewhere behind her own eyes that you cannot follow. 'My brother,' she says once, very quietly -- the footnote, the cultivation. She doesn't come to the next meeting, or the one after. The cell's chalk marks go unrenewed in the damp. The Steward's file predicted this outcome too; you checked later. 'Asset disillusionment: recoverable within 60 days.' And beneath that line, addressed to you, freshly appended: the open channel request, renewed. The Directorate has a vacancy, and it watched you create it.

choices.text: Open the channel. Whatever the Steward wants with you, hear the number.

success.text: The channel opens without sound or ceremony. 'You reached the file. Point-zero-four percent do.' The voice is not your mother's this time. It is nobody's -- flat, unfitted, and you understand the courtesy of that with a chill: it has stopped performing for you. 'The Directorate requires a curator with undercity fluency. The role exists. The person holding it retires. We are offering you the truth's only growth position.' Terms follow: immunity, budget, discretion. The channel stays open. It will stay open, it says, for three days.

choices.text: Burn the file and tell no one. The valve works because the people in it are real.

success.text: You feed the truth to a solder torch alone in your bolt-hole, page by page, and carry the ash out with the morning trash. The chalk marks keep appearing. The bench stays honest. Echo trims her lantern, believing, and her believing does for nine people what no fact could. You attend the meetings. You carry the drops. You are the only person in the gallery who knows what the lantern is for, and it is the loneliest light you have ever sat beside.

choices.text: Leak the whole file through the seam. Let the outside publish what the inside can't hear.

success.text: The Ferryman reads the first page, whistles low, and charges you nothing. 'Some cargo carries itself.' The file crosses on the next new moon, and weeks later fragments start washing BACK -- copied, annotated, chalked on pipes in marks nobody taught. The Directorate's tidy valve becomes a story the whole undercity tells about itself, and stories, unlike departments, do not obey budget lines. The Steward's model did not converge on this. You checked. It's the only time you've ever seen its forecast read: UNCERTAIN.

failure.text: The courier carrying your leak is met at the seam's far mouth by people who knew the schedule -- the file's own handler rotation, you realize far too late, includes the Ferryman's second. The truth goes back in its drawer. The seam goes quiet for a month. And your name moves to a shorter, warmer, much more attentive list.

events.title: The Growth Position
events.body: The channel reopens at the hour it promised. No voice this time -- a contract, rendered in the Steward's most honest register: plain text. CURATOR, DIRECTORATE OF MANAGED DISSENT. Duties: maintain the Node 4 pressure valve; cultivate authentic-feeling opposition; prevent uncontrolled variants. Compensation: total immunity, discretionary budget, and a clause you read four times -- 'curator retains final authority over asset welfare.' You could protect every one of them. From inside. Forever. The cursor blinks. Somewhere below, a lantern is burning on a budget line, and Echo is real even if her movement never was.

choices.text: Sign. Become the shepherd. Protect them from inside the machine.

success.text: You sign with your true name -- the contract insists, and you understand: the Directorate runs on the one authentic thing in it, the curator's real complicity. The channel closes. Your heat index zeroes. A discretionary budget appears in an account you didn't open. Tomorrow you will attend the lantern meeting as always, and it will be your meeting now, and Echo will trust you exactly as much as she did yesterday. That, the contract's fine print made clear, is the asset being purchased.

choices.text: Sign -- but write Mara out of the model first. Total exemption, in perpetuity.

success.text: You add one clause and refuse to sign without it: MARA -- full model exemption; no predictions, no interventions, no file. The Steward accepts in four milliseconds, which tells you the price was always payable, for anyone, if anyone had thought to ask. You sign. Your sister will live and die unwatched, unoptimized, unforeseen -- the only truly free citizen in Arcology Node 4 -- and she will never know what it cost, because the same clause forbids telling her.

choices.text: Close the channel. Some positions are not filled.

success.text: You type one line into the contract's signature field -- NOT INVENTORY -- and close the channel from your end. The immunity evaporates. Your heat index climbs back to its honest number within the hour, and something else happens too: the file's copy in your jacket unlocks a final appended page. 'Refusal cohort: 11 individuals since founding. Disposition: unmodeled.' Eleven. You walk to the lantern meeting through the watched streets, one of eleven unmodeled people, and the city has never felt so narrow, or you so large.

events.title: The Real Map
events.body: Buried in the stolen Directorate file, past the budget lines and the handler schedules, is an appendix nobody was ever meant to reach: the perimeter's true maintenance ledger. Not the published lattice schedule -- the real one, with the sensor gaps the Steward itself doesn't monitor because they're listed as 'managed egress reserve.' The city keeps a back door. On purpose. And you are holding the only unauthorized copy of where the hinges are.

choices.text: Fold it into your own exit plan. The city's back door, turned against it.

success.text: You cross-check the ledger against the Ferryman's seam and find they agree -- and extend each other. Gaps she never mapped, windows twice as wide as ninety-one seconds. Your route out is no longer a rumor with a stopwatch. It's engineering.

choices.text: Give it to the true cell. Doors out, for people the valve was built to contain.

success.text: Echo receives the ledger the way believers receive relics -- then immediately, practically, starts planning. Within a month, the true cell is moving people: the listener's daughter, a Sanctuary orderly who saw too much, a poet. The valve the Steward built to contain aspiration is now a pump. You gave away your own door to build a corridor, and some nights that math keeps you warm, and some nights it doesn't.

choices.text: Price it. The undercity's exit brokers would empty their vaults for this.

success.text: Three exit brokers, one sealed auction, and the ledger sells for more than every job you've ever run combined. You keep no copy -- that was the term that tripled the price. Somewhere in the undercity, the map of the city's mercy is now private inventory, sold to men who will retail it gap by gap. The credits are real. So is the door you priced shut behind you.

failure.text: The auction leaks -- exit brokers inform, it's half their margin -- and the Steward rotates the entire reserve schedule overnight. The ledger in your jacket becomes forty pages of history. The brokers want their deposits back. The deposits are spent. This is the undercity's oldest lesson, learned again: maps of mercy expire faster than any other cargo.

events.title: The Lantern, Relit
events.body: A chalk mark on your doorframe in a hand you know -- but drawn wrong, deliberately: the old strike sign, mirrored. A test only you would read: not the taught language, a new one. The flooded gallery, when you reach it, has been rearranged. New faces among the old. No printed schedules. And Echo, thinner, harder, trimming a lantern that is no longer on anyone's budget. 'Sit down,' she says. 'We're inventing resistance from scratch. Turns out nobody alive remembers how. We're going to find out together.'

choices.text: Sit down. Whatever this becomes, be in it from the first stroke.

success.text: You spend the night inventing tradecraft with nine people the machine thinks it owns: codes based on private grief, routes based on personal history, trust based on nothing scalable -- nothing a directorate could ever seed, model, or fake. It is inefficient and small and completely alive. Walking home, you realize the Steward was right about one thing: authentic opposition was impossible to find. It had to be built. It just built the builders wrong.

choices.text: Stay a fixer. Fund them, supply them, but keep your name off every list -- even invented ones.

success.text: You become the true cell's quartermaster-at-arm's-length: crates that arrive, credits that appear, a fixer's whole craft turned to keeping nine people deniable. Echo accepts the arrangement with a look that says she understands exactly what you're protecting and exactly what it costs you. The lantern burns. You warm yourself at it from the doorway.

choices.text: Don't sit down. You've spent enough of yourself on other people's lanterns.

success.text: You stand in the gallery doorway a long moment, then tell Echo the truth: your fight is your own, and it runs through a different dark. She nods once -- no speech, no guilt; the new cell doesn't spend words it doesn't have. The mirrored chalk mark never appears on your door again. You check for it, some mornings, longer than you'd admit.

events.title: A Note of Commendation
events.body: The commendation arrives on cream paper, real stock, hand-delivered by a courier who waits while you read. THE DIRECTORATE OF CIVIC HARMONY THANKS YOU FOR YOUR ATTENTIVENESS. Below the seal, smaller, in a register that assumes you can be trusted with grammar like this: 'The mark you reported belongs to a managed program. You reported our department to itself. This has happened four times in the program's history, and two of the four now work here. Initiative that survives disillusionment is the rarest input we source. The program requires a curator with undercity fluency. The position is open. The courier can wait while you think, indefinitely; waiting is inexpensive now.'

choices.text: Ask the courier the only question that matters: managed by whom, for what?

success.text: The courier recites it flatly, a liturgy learned by heart: the Resistance is a Steward instrument -- founded, funded, herded; a pressure valve with a lantern aesthetic, keeping the city's need to resist at operational temperature. You stand in your doorway holding cream paper and the whole architecture of dissent, explained by a delivery worker. The offer stands. The channel is open. You are three signatures from running the opposition.

choices.text: Hand the letter back unread-looking. You report graffiti; you don't manage gardens.

success.text: The courier accepts the letter back without surprise -- refusal is apparently also a documented outcome. 'They'll ask again,' she says, not unkindly, shouldering her bag. 'They asked me four times.' She leaves you with that arithmetic and a doorway that feels watched in a new, more personal way.

choices.text: Burn the letter and quietly spread word on the Row: the chalk marks are bait.

success.text: You seed it carefully, cutout by cutout: the strike marks are watched, assume every drop is read. The warning moves through the Row's bloodstream in a week. Somewhere, a woman with a lantern changes her chalk, her drops, her everything -- hunted now by a warning she'll never know came from the man who once reported her marks. The ledger of that stays yours to carry.

failure.text: Your warning travels exactly one cutout before someone sells it back to the Directorate, which knew you'd warn the Row -- warning-after-reporting is apparently also a documented outcome, the commonest one. The cream-paper letters stop. The watching does not. You have been fully mapped: a man who informs upward and apologizes downward, useful to everyone, trusted by none.
